accuracy.reason: All nine objectives are supported: partition-conditional impossibility, live disconnected nodes, real-time single-copy order, eventual successful request completion, missing-information proof, safe majority progress, divergent local progress, conditional convergence and operation-level choices. The quorum example explicitly requires an agreement protocol; no counting-only consistency guarantee or automatic safe merge is asserted.

evidence.quote: Overlapping operations may be placed in either order, provided the resulting order is valid for one copy. The required order follows completed-before-started relationships, not a globally synchronized timestamp on every request.
Convergence means agreement on a resulting state. It does not promise that every conflicting edit survives; the conflict-resolution policy determines the result.

mechanisms.reason: Confirmed remote write then isolated read makes the impossible choice traceable, including why guesses and blocking the original write fail. The live-node, old/new value and 2-of-3 diagrams faithfully show those states. Reconciliation and lost intent explain consequences beyond slogans; learner transfers 10/12 to 0/1 correctly.

evidence.quote: Server A accepts a change to 12 and confirms success. Then a client reads from Server B. B still knows only 10.
Guessing the new value cannot guarantee correctness across possible unseen writes. The obstacle is missing information, not a particular database product.

coherence.reason: Distributed communication and partition definitions precede C and A; the proof uses those prerequisites before contrasting CP/AP behavior, convergence and decisions. All card questions can be answered in sequence. The final examples use already-explained staleness, waiting and reconciliation.

evidence.quote: Prevents parts of a system from exchanging messages. Servers on both sides can still be running and receiving requests.
Outside partitions, CAP does not force a choice between consistency and availability. It does not predict normal-operation latency, capacity or operating cost; evaluate those separately.

decisions.reason: Makes operation-specific consistency versus completion costs explicit, allows safe work elsewhere, separates stale reads from conflicting accepted writes and requires a resolution policy after healing. Profile/reservation/offline examples expose user consequences. CAP is expressly insufficient for healthy latency/capacity/cost decisions.

evidence.quote: Availability supplies no automatic safe merge. Selecting one conflicting value can lose another user's intent, and cross-record rules require their own protection.
Outside partitions, CAP does not force a choice between consistency and availability. It does not predict normal-operation latency, capacity or operating cost; evaluate those separately.

clarity.reason: Linearizability, quorum, partition and convergence receive concise operational definitions. The arithmetic example and diagrams clarify the information barrier without distracting setup. Distinctions from timestamps, uptime, ACID validity and immediate read-your-writes remove common ambiguities without requiring outside knowledge.

evidence.quote: CAP availability does not mean fast, immediately answered, or a particular uptime percentage. The theorem requires eventual per-request completion and sets no practical response-time target.
Eventually gives no fixed deadline or immediate read-your-writes guarantee. Applications must decide whether temporary older reads are acceptable.

outcomes.reason: Actual learner explains networked copies and coordination, conditional C/A impossibility, why choose-any-two misleads, live reachable disconnected nodes, partition-tolerant behavior and unavoidable communication risk. Exact quotes entail all six criteria.

Covers real-time linearizability, post-write read with no intervening write, valid ordering of overlap, distinction from convergence/ACID rules, eventual successful completion without latency bound, failed/refused/indefinitely waiting operations and uptime distinction. All six are taught, not inferred from prior expertise.

Correctly transfers the slide to B knowing 0 while consistency requires 1; old value violates C, refusal/indefinite wait loses A, and guessing cannot work across indistinguishable unseen writes. Exact evidence supports all three criteria.

Explains safe-order operations versus unsafe waiting/failure, partial majority progress, local stale reads, conflicting writes, explicit post-healing reconciliation and lack of automatic intent/invariant preservation. Covers all six criteria with correctly scoped majority example.

States quiescence, resumed communication and completed propagation/reconciliation conditions; no fixed deadline, immediate own-write visibility or universal intent preservation. Compares strict refusal/delay with local stale service, addresses recovery and client effects, and scopes guarantees to operation/configuration separately from normal cost/latency. Notes absent algorithm rather than inventing one.

sourceChecks.claim: Gilbert/Lynch abstract and formal theorem support conditional inability to guarantee atomic reads/writes and availability under message loss.
Formal partition model loses cross-component messages; live processes may continue. More nodes do not repair communication.
Formal atomic object definition supports real-time order and completed-write visibility; overlap need only admit a valid total order, without shared clocks.
Formal availability requires eventual termination at non-failing nodes with an operation response, without a latency bound; a refused read is not a returned value.
Proof partitions nodes, completes a write, then uses an indistinguishable isolated read execution to derive contradiction. Both diagram values and guessing explanation preserve that reasoning.
Raft paper section 2 supports safety under partitions and progress with communicating majority; slide limits its 2-of-3 illustration to majority agreement, not arbitrary replicas.
Eric Brewer authored the linked primary essay; partition management/recovery and invariants sections support local progress, conflict reconciliation and possible lost intent.

AWS confirms eventual reads can miss completed writes and supported per-operation strong-read options. Conditional convergence and reconciliation limits also follow the checked Brewer recovery discussion; no AWS timing or all-intent guarantee imported.
Brewer explains fine-grained choices by operation/data and explicit recovery; healthy systems can provide C and A. The theorem alone does not calculate workload capacity or cost.
